doc.title: Ray Drummond interviewed by Monk Rowe, Toronto, Canada, January 9, 2003

title: Lincoln's Gettysburg Address on his website
summary: He explains why the Gettysburg Address matters to him, as the end of secession and a challenge of national redress.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Politics, race and the state of the country

blocks.x: I was looking at your website and —
I found it interesting that you put Lincoln’s Gettysburg Address in there.
That’s mine. That’s the current offering.
It’s really interesting to revisit that speech now. Did you come across it again and then make a connection or is it something you thought of?

No it’s something — the Gettysburg Address for me has always been a very important thing, not because it signaled the end of slavery, it didn’t, also it signaled the end of separatism, meaning the south asserting its contention that as a Confederate group of — not states, I don’t want to call them states — provinces or as a group of individual former states that we have the right to separate ourself out even though we said initially that we were going to part of this United States. Just because we don’t like the way you guys are telling us how we’re supposed to be running our affairs down here, that included slavery, quote states’ rights. I mean a lot of people, it’s you know, I mean that’s one of the crosses

that we bear as Americans anyway, trying to figure out our sins that we need to really atone for. Because we haven’t atoned — I mean slavery is one of them, various other things that we’ve done to people, I’m talking about within our country under the guise of either states’ rights or the majority rules or whatever. I mean there are several levels of redress that we still need to address as a nation. So to me that has always been the epitome of one of the challenges that still remains in front of us. Lincoln threw down — basically he said look this is what this nation is really all about and so that’s what you need to keep in front of you. So no matter what you do and no matter what you start to — when you start to bow down to those who have died, who have laid their lives down for us to get this far, you now, don’t forget this is where we’re supposed to be going. No matter where you think we’ve been or where you think we are, that’s where we need to go. And that is, ever since I first heard the Gettysburg Address in elementary school it always stuck with me. It’s like damn, that is the shit. That’s the shit. When I grow up that’s what I want to do for a living.
